title: Atoms, Isotopes and the Mole

cards.b:
A single drop of water holds more than a billion billion molecules. Chemists cannot count atoms one by one, so they invented a counting unit, the mole. It is the bridge between the invisible world of atoms and the grams you weigh on a lab balance.

First, though, we need to know what an atom is.

An atom has a tiny dense nucleus with protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral), and electrons (negative) around it. The atom is mostly empty space: if the nucleus were a marble, the atom would be a stadium.

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. It defines the element.
  • Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
  • A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons.

Example: sodium, Z = 11, A = 23, so it has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons.

• John Dalton, 1808: atoms are the basic building blocks; each element has its own kind.
  • J.J. Thomson, 1897: discovered the electron.
  • Ernest Rutherford, 1911: gold-foil experiment showed a small dense nucleus (proton named about 1919).
  • James Chadwick, 1932: discovered the neutron.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Same protons, so same chemistry, but different mass.

  • Hydrogen: protium (0 neutrons), deuterium (1), tritium (2).
  • Carbon-12 and carbon-14. Carbon-14 is radioactive and used in dating old remains.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

This is why the periodic table shows chlorine as 35.5: it is a weighted average. Chlorine is about 75 percent Cl-35 and 25 percent Cl-37. Average = 0.75 x 35 + 0.25 x 37 = 35.5.

One carbon-12 atom is defined as exactly 12 atomic mass units. We weigh atoms relative to it.

The mole is a count: 6.022 x 10^23 particles, called the Avogadro constant (named after Amedeo Avogadro, whose 1811 idea about gases inspired it). A mole of carbon-12 weighs exactly 12 g.

So the molar mass in g/mol equals the atomic or molecular mass in units. Dozen = 12 things; mole = 6.022 x 10^23 things.

Three relations cover most problems.

Formulas

moles = mass (g) / molar mass (g/mol)

number of particles = moles x 6.022 x 10^23

molar mass of a compound = sum of atomic masses

Water: H2O = 2 x 1 + 16 = 18 g/mol. CO2 = 12 + 2 x 16 = 44 g/mol. NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol.

How many moles and molecules are in 36 g of water?

  1. Molar mass of water = 18 g/mol.
  2. Moles = 36 / 18 = 2 mol.
  3. Molecules = 2 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 1.2 x 10^24.

Another: how many grams in 0.5 mol of NaCl? Mass = 0.5 x 58.5 = 29.25 g.

• A mole is not a mass. It is a number. A mole of feathers and a mole of lead have the same count, different masses.
  • Isotopes are not different elements. They differ only in neutrons.
  • Atoms are not solid balls. They are mostly empty space.
  • Mass number is not atomic mass exactly. Mass number is a whole count; atomic mass is a measured average.

Long before Dalton, the Vaisheshika school in ancient India, associated with the philosopher Kanada, argued that matter is made of indivisible particles called paramanu. It was philosophy, not experiment, but it shows early atomic thinking.

In modern times, India runs heavy-water plants under the Department of Atomic Energy. Heavy water contains deuterium, the hydrogen isotope with one neutron, and is used as a moderator in India's pressurised heavy-water reactors.

• Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
  • Isotopes share protons but differ in neutrons.
  • 1 mole = 6.022 x 10^23 particles; molar mass links grams to moles.
  • moles = mass / molar mass.

Think about it

1. Why do isotopes of one element behave almost identically in chemical reactions?

2. Which has more atoms: 12 g of carbon or 12 g of magnesium (24 g/mol)?
